title: Beeswax lip balm and furniture polish
subtitle: Two simple recipes for rendered beeswax from the hive.
excerpt: Filtered beeswax from your hive has two good small-batch uses beyond candles: a simple lip balm with a carrier oil, and a traditional furniture polish with linseed or turpentine. Both recipes require clean, rendered wax and take under 30 minutes. Neither requires specialist equipment.
sourceNotes: Vivienne Munn, The Beekeeper's Bible (2010), wax products chapter. Mrs Beeton, Book of Household Management (1861), furniture care section (Project Gutenberg #10136). DIY Natural, Beeswax lip balm tutorial (2022).

glossaryTerms.definition: A plant-based oil (coconut, sweet almond, castor, jojoba) used to dilute beeswax in cosmetic recipes, creating a smooth, spreadable product.

content.text: Both recipes start from the same point: rendered, filtered beeswax. Poorly filtered wax with propolis and debris in it will produce a cloudy or gritty lip balm and a dull polish. Take the time to filter properly before proceeding.
20 g filtered beeswax, grated or chopped into small pieces
30 g coconut oil or sweet almond oil (
Optional: 5 g castor oil (adds gloss), a few drops of honey (adds very slight sweetness)
Melt wax in a small glass bowl over hot water (double boiler). Add the carrier oil once the wax is liquid and stir to combine.
Add optional castor oil and honey if using. Stir well.
Pour immediately into small lip balm pots or sterilised jam jars. The mixture sets quickly. Cap when just starting to firm at the surface. Makes 4 to 5 standard lip balm pots (5 ml each).
Test consistency once set: rub a small amount on the back of your hand. If it is too hard and waxy, melt down and add more carrier oil. If it is too soft and greasy, melt down and add more wax.
Turpentine is flammable and its vapour is unpleasant to inhale. Work with good ventilation. Do not heat turpentine directly over a flame.
100 ml pure turpentine (not white spirit) or raw linseed oil
Melt the wax over a double boiler and remove from heat. Allow to cool to 50 to 55 C.
Pour turpentine slowly into the warm wax and stir well. Work quickly as the mixture stiffens as it cools. Pour into a wide-mouthed glass jar and allow to set completely.
To use: apply a thin layer with a soft cloth, work into the grain, and buff off after 10 to 15 minutes. Builds up a deep patina with repeated applications.

attrs.cue: Lip balm is too grainy or has visible particles
attrs.cause: Wax not fully filtered, or wax and oil not fully combined before pouring
attrs.fix: Re-melt, strain through muslin cloth, stir more thoroughly, and repour. Ensure both wax and oil are at the same temperature before combining.

attrs.cue: Polish left a whitish bloom on the furniture surface
attrs.cause: Too much wax applied, or applied on a cold day when it could not absorb into the wood
attrs.fix: Buff vigorously with a dry lint-free cloth. Apply thinner coats next time and work into warmer wood.
